prompt_text: How do I start an Airbnb rental arbitrage business and what tools and data should I use?
answer_verbatim:
To start an **Airbnb rental arbitrage** business, first confirm the property can legally be used as a short-term rental, then find a market where projected Airbnb revenue exceeds your rent and operating costs, and only then secure written landlord permission before signing a lease.[1][2][4][14] The core workflow is: **research → underwrite → get approval → furnish → launch → optimize**.[1][2][6]

A practical step-by-step approach looks like this:

- **Check legality first.** Verify local short-term rental rules, zoning, and any HOA or building restrictions before spending time on a deal.[1][7][19]
- **Pick a market with demand.** Look for areas with strong nightly rates and occupancy, and avoid markets where regulations are too restrictive.[1][7][12]
- **Underwrite the deal.** Estimate monthly revenue using average daily rate and occupancy, then subtract rent, utilities, cleaning, platform fees, supplies, insurance, and maintenance.[1][7][19]
- **Get landlord approval in writing.** Ask for permission to sublet or use the unit for short-term rentals, and put any revenue split or special terms in writing.[1][18][20]
- **Set up the business.** Many guides recommend forming an LLC, getting an EIN, and opening a separate business bank account before launch.[5][6][13]
- **Furnish and prepare the unit.** Outfit the property for guest use, take professional photos, and create a strong listing.[1][16]
- **Launch with systems.** Use cleaning schedules, guest messaging SOPs, and pricing automation so the business can run consistently.[2][5][16]

For **tools and data**, the most useful setup is:

| Need | Best data/tools to use | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|
| **Market demand** | Airbnb search results, AirDNA, Mashvisor, AllTheRooms | Shows nightly rates, occupancy, and demand by area.[3][6][7][19] |
| **Comparable long-term rent** | Zillow, Apartments.com, local listings | Lets you measure the spread between rent and expected STR revenue.[3] |
| **Regulatory checks** | City rules, council records, HOA documents, local news | Helps avoid illegal or high-risk markets.[1][19] |
| **Profit analysis** | Spreadsheet or underwriting model | Lets you test rent, occupancy, ADR, fees, and startup costs.[1][7][19] |
| **Pricing automation** | Dynamic pricing software | Adjusts rates based on demand and occupancy.[16] |
| **Operations** | STR management software, cleaning/turnover tools, guest messaging tools | Reduces day-to-day workload and improves consistency.[2][5] |

The key numbers to track are **average daily rate (ADR)**, **occupancy rate**, **monthly rent**, **startup costs**, and **all operating expenses**.[1][7][19] One guide recommends looking for a projected revenue-to-rent ratio of at least **1.5x to 2x** before moving forward.[3][5][19]

A simple underwriting formula from the sources is:

\[
(\text{ADR} \times \text{Occupancy Rate}) - (\text{Monthly Rent} + \text{Operating Expenses}) = \text{Monthly Profit}
\][1]
